doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Steve Lacy, Hiram Bullock, Delmar Brown and what Levin learned from Gil
summary: Gil found young and unusual players such as Steve Lacy, Hiram Bullock and Delmar Brown; Levin describes what he took from the band.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: I mean they just all think and play and perform with the same — it’s like one head. Sometimes somebody conducts, sometimes they don’t even bother. They just do it and the sax section blends so well. It’s just great. That’s the way you do a big band. Gil, it just never occurred to him. There was one European tour we did, the band was a little bigger than usual but the sax section was Dave Sanborn, Arthur Blythe, Steve Lacy and Howard Johnson and George Adams. Now these, Howard playing baritone sax — he plays it but he’s a tuba player and he plays with a lot of spirit on baritone but he doesn’t blend with anything. Steve does what he does. Sanborn, who has changed the way the instrument is played but forget any concept of blending. It was okay. It was okay. It was great. Because any one of them that would stand up to take a solo he would tear the place apart. It was a great tour. But what an awful choice of five guys for a sax section. But that’s what Gil did. He found Steve Lacy way, way back. Steve was just wandering around doing, I think he was starting to do the Thelonious Monk thing that he got into and expounded so well. And Gil just brought him into a recording session, some big record date, nobody knew who he was, and this guy who played weird stuff on soprano sax, a “weasel horn” Howard Johnson calls it. Steve was accepted into it, and some of his recordings like “Sketches of Spain” or “Porgy & Bess,” it’s great, with the digital reproductions of them they’ve gone back and dug out those masters and in some ways the LPs sound real classic. But they were victims of — they had to do a lot of compression to LPs back then so a lot of the quieter sounds were kind of squashed out of the picture. The CDs it’s all there. It may not be the way you’re used to hearing them, or the way you’d rather hear them, but you can hear everything. And every once in a while you’ll hear like a second trombone player, he’s just got a couple of notes and he’ll just tie into it [scats] it’ll come out. And this is not a guy that is not a great blender. I don’t know who it would be but he was there because Gil liked the way he played. I came into the band, which I think is typical of Gil’s attitude of first of all getting interesting players. If he liked the way they played, if he heard a blues element in their playing or something soulful, you’re in the band. I’ll write a part for you. He just liked me, which, I’m beyond honored. So there was this aspect also of where he would find young players or developing players and just put them in the band and bring them along and give them opportunities that were invaluable, I mean just invaluable. I couldn’t begin to assess, even at this point, what I got out of being in that band for that long, the tremendous help that it was to me, not just career, I mean it changed the way I think about music, about the way I play, the way I write, everything. There still is, what twelve, thirteen years since we’ve lost Gil, I still never sit down at an instrument with a piece of score paper without having some of Gil’s influence to show up in it. Oh what else. People — Hiram Bullock came into the band at one point. Hiram is not a jazz player and he’s the first one to admit it. Gil I think heard a

lot of Jimi Hendrix in Hiram’s playing. Not the exact notes or the riffs just the spirit that Hiram plays with. And Hiram does what he does and a lot of people didn’t like it. A lot of people didn’t like it. Audience. The band — we had a great time. And Hiram I remember him saying man, I don’t know what I’m doing in this band but I’m here. And Gil wrote for him, he featured him, he liked the way he played. And Delmar Brown was another one. Delmar is a wonderful player. He’s not real good at playing other people’s music. Gil loved the way he played. You’re in the band.
